lead: This unit turns a transfer function into pictures: how a system responds to sine waves, and how Bode, polar and Nyquist plots show stability and margins. After it you can read frequency-domain specifications, sketch the three standard plots, apply the Nyquist criterion, and use M circles and the Nichols chart to estimate closed-loop response.
about: The unit starts with the sinusoidal steady-state response and the specifications Mr, ωr and bandwidth in 4.1. Chapter 4.2 connects these to overshoot, peak time and settling time for second-order systems. Chapters 4.3 and 4.4 turn G(jω) into Bode and polar plots. Chapter 4.5 adds the Nyquist contour and the encirclement criterion for closed-loop stability. Chapter 4.6 reads gain and phase margins from the same plots. Chapter 4.7 closes the loop by mapping the open-loop plot to closed-loop M and N circles and the Nichols chart, giving bandwidth and resonant peak without solving the closed-loop transfer function each time.

chapters.idea: A stable linear system responds to a sine wave with a sine wave of the same frequency, scaled by |G(jω)| and shifted by ∠G(jω).
chapters.depth: Define the sinusoidal transfer function G(jω)=G(s) with s=jω. Derive the steady-state result for input A sin(ωt): output A|G(jω)| sin(ωt+∠G(jω)). Cover frequency-domain specifications: resonant peak Mr, resonant frequency ωr, bandwidth ωb, cut-off frequency, gain crossover ωgc and phase crossover ωpc. For the standard second-order system G(jω)=ωn²/((jω)²+2ζωn(jω)+ωn²), derive magnitude M=1/√((1−r²)²+(2ζr)²) with r=ω/ωn, and phase −tan⁻¹(2ζr/(1−r²)). Give Mr=1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)) for ζ<1/√2, ωr=ωn√(1−2ζ²), and ωb=ωn√((1−2ζ²)+√((1−2ζ²)²+1)). Some syllabi call G(jω) the sinusoidal transfer function.

figure.aria: A magnitude curve for a second-order system with damping ratio 0.3, rising to a resonant peak near 1.75 and then falling.

chapters.example: A unity-feedback second-order system has G(s)=100/(s²+6s+100). Find ζ, ωn, Mr, ωr, ωb, and the steady-state output for input r(t)=2 sin(9t). Answer: ωn=10 rad/s, ζ=0.3, Mr=1.75, ωr=9.06 rad/s, ωb=14.54 rad/s, output 3.49 sin(9t−70.6°).
chapters.trap: Frequency response is the steady-state response, not the transient response. Do not confuse ωr with ωn, and remember Mr and ωr exist only when ζ<1/√2. Bandwidth is measured from the zero-frequency magnitude, not from the resonant peak.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 transfer functions; Unit 2 second-order response; complex numbers.
chapters.leave: Bode, polar and Nyquist construction to 4.3–4.5; controller design to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: For a second-order system, frequency-domain numbers such as Mr and bandwidth translate directly into time-domain numbers such as overshoot and settling time.
chapters.depth: Build the exact second-order links: Mr=1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)), ωr=ωn√(1−2ζ²), bandwidth formula from 4.1, percentage overshoot Mp=100 exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)), peak time tp=π/(ωn√(1−ζ²)), and 2% settling time ts≈4/(ζωn). Explain the trend: smaller ζ gives larger Mr and larger overshoot; larger ωn gives wider bandwidth and faster response. Include the approximate rule Mr≈1/(2ζ) for small ζ and PM≈100ζ degrees as a rough guide only. State that these exact links are for second-order systems; for higher-order systems use dominant poles and check with 4.7.

figure.aria: A mapping from damping ratio 0.4 to resonant peak and overshoot, and from bandwidth to settling time.

chapters.example: A unity-feedback second-order system has ζ=0.4 and ωn=5 rad/s. Find Mr, ωr, bandwidth, percentage overshoot, peak time, and 2% settling time. Answer: Mr=1.36, ωr=4.12 rad/s, ωb=6.87 rad/s, overshoot=25.4%, tp=0.685 s, ts=2 s.
chapters.trap: The formulas fail outside the second-order model. Do not use Mr=1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)) for ζ≥0.707, and do not apply second-order settling-time formulas blindly to a higher-order system with a slow pole or zero.
chapters.leave: Higher-order exact correlation to 4.7; compensator design to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A Bode plot separates gain and phase into two curves against log frequency, so multiplication in G(jω) becomes addition of straight-line segments.
chapters.depth: Define gain in decibels: 20 log₁₀|G(jω)|. Use a logarithmic frequency axis. Cover standard factors: constant K; pole or zero at the origin; simple pole or zero (1+jωT)^±1; quadratic factor (1+2ζ(jω/ωn)+(jω/ωn)²)^±1. Give corner frequencies, asymptotic slopes ±20 dB/decade per simple pole or zero and ±40 dB/decade per quadratic pair, and phase contributions. Teach sketching rules for typical systems, including initial slope from the number of poles at the origin. Show stability reading from gain crossover and phase crossover, but leave margin formulas to 4.6. Include finding a transfer function from a Bode plot when the asymptotes are given. Some syllabi call this the Bode plot approach.

figure.aria: Straight-line Bode magnitude asymptotes: flat at 20 dB, then falling 20 dB per decade after 1 rad/s and 40 dB per decade after 10 rad/s.

chapters.example: Sketch the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot of G(s)=100/((s+1)(s+10)). Mark the corner frequencies, low-frequency gain and slopes, then find the exact gain crossover frequency and phase there. Answer: low-frequency gain 20 dB; corners at 1 and 10 rad/s; slopes 0, −20 and −40 dB/decade; exact ωgc≈7.8 rad/s; phase at ωgc≈−121°.
chapters.trap: Magnitude in dB uses 20 log₁₀, not 10 log₁₀. The corner of (1+jωT) is at ω=1/T, and slopes are per decade, not per octave. An asymptotic 0 dB crossing is only an estimate; a nearby corner can move the exact gain crossover.
chapters.prereq: 4.1; Unit 1 transfer function; logarithms and decibels.
chapters.leave: Nyquist encirclements to 4.5; margin definitions to 4.6; compensator design to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A polar plot draws G(jω) as a complex vector locus while ω runs from 0 to ∞, showing magnitude and phase together in one curve.
chapters.depth: Write G(jω)=X(ω)+jY(ω). Teach start and end points for Type 0, Type 1 and Type 2 systems: each pole at the origin adds −90° phase and sends magnitude to infinity at ω=0. Cover standard shapes, intersection with the real axis by setting Im G(jω)=0, intersection with the imaginary axis by setting Re G(jω)=0, and the significance of the polar plot for reading gain and phase. Some syllabi call it the polar plot or the frequency locus. Keep full encirclement and the Nyquist criterion for 4.5.

figure.aria: Polar plot starting far down the negative imaginary axis, crossing the negative real axis at −1/6, and ending at the origin from the positive imaginary side.

chapters.example: Sketch the polar plot of G(s)=1/(s(s+1)(s+2)). Find its start, end, and real-axis crossing. Answer: at ω→0+, |G|→∞ and phase→−90°; at ω→∞, G→0 with phase +90°; real-axis crossing at ω=√2 rad/s with G=−1/6.
chapters.trap: The polar plot uses ω from 0 to ∞ only. Do not include negative frequencies unless the question asks for a Nyquist plot. A pole at the origin makes the starting magnitude infinite; do not draw it from a finite point.
chapters.leave: Encirclement count and Nyquist criterion to 4.5; margins to 4.6.

chapters.idea: The Nyquist plot closes the open-loop frequency locus over a contour that encloses the right half-plane, and the number of encirclements of −1 gives closed-loop stability.
chapters.depth: Define the Nyquist contour: the jω axis from −∞ to +∞ plus a large right-half-plane semicircle, with small detours around open-loop poles on the imaginary axis. Map this contour through G(s)H(s). State the criterion clearly: let N be the number of clockwise encirclements of −1 by the open-loop Nyquist plot, P the number of open-loop poles in the right half-plane, and Z the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane. Then Z=N+P; closed-loop stability needs Z=0. Cover Type 0, Type 1 and Type 2 plots, relative stability, and the effect of gain K. Some syllabi call this the Nyquist stability criterion.

figure.aria: Nyquist plot for K=6 crossing the critical point −1 on the negative real axis, with its mirror image below.

chapters.example: For G(s)H(s)=K/(s(s+1)(s+2)), use the Nyquist criterion to find the range of K for closed-loop stability. Answer: the negative-real-axis crossing is at −K/6; with P=0, the critical gain is K=6, so 0<K<6 is stable and K=6 is marginal.
chapters.trap: The sign of encirclements is the main trap. Fix one convention and state it: here N is clockwise and Z=N+P. Also P counts open-loop right-half-plane poles, not closed-loop poles. Poles on the jω axis need a detour, and a point exactly at −1 is marginal.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 polar plot; Unit 3 Routh-Hurwitz and characteristic equation; complex mapping.
chapters.leave: Margin formulas to 4.6; Nichols chart to 4.7; internal stability and state-space tests to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Gain margin and phase margin measure how far the open-loop plot is from the critical point −1, and so how much gain or phase can be added before instability.
chapters.depth: Define gain crossover frequency ωgc by |G(jωgc)H(jωgc)|=1, and phase crossover frequency ωpc by ∠G(jωpc)H(jωpc)=−180°. Define gain margin GM=−20 log₁₀|G(jωpc)H(jωpc)| dB and phase margin PM=180°+∠G(jωgc)H(jωgc). Explain physical meaning: GM is the extra gain factor before marginal stability; PM is the extra phase lag that can be tolerated. State that for a stable minimum-phase open-loop system, positive GM and PM mean closed-loop stability; zero means marginal; negative means unstable. Note GM can be infinite when phase never reaches −180°. Read both margins from Bode and Nyquist plots.

figure.aria: Bode magnitude and phase curves for G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)); the magnitude crosses 0 dB near 2.10 rad/s and the phase crosses −180° at 3.16 rad/s.

chapters.example: For G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)), find the gain crossover frequency, phase crossover frequency, gain margin and phase margin. Answer: ωgc≈2.10 rad/s, ωpc=√10≈3.16 rad/s, GM≈6.85 dB, PM≈13.6°.
chapters.trap: Do not swap the two crossover frequencies: GM uses the phase crossover, PM uses the gain crossover. GM is −20 log₁₀|G(jωpc)|, not +20 log₁₀. Margins read from Bode plots assume a minimum-phase stable open loop; for open-loop unstable systems use the Nyquist encirclement count in 4.5.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 Bode plot, 4.5 Nyquist plot; Unit 3 stability.
chapters.leave: Compensator design to Unit 5; Nichols chart reading to 4.7.

chapters.idea: Constant closed-loop magnitude M and phase N contours drawn in the open-loop plane, and the Nichols chart, convert an open-loop frequency response into closed-loop response without solving for T(s).
chapters.depth: For unity feedback, T(jω)=G(jω)/(1+G(jω)); M=|T| and N=∠T. Derive the M-circle equation: with G=X+jY, (X+M²/(M²−1))²+Y²=(M/(M²−1))² for M≠1, and the M=1 line X=−1/2. Give N circles from N=tan(∠T) without full algebra. Introduce the Nichols chart: open-loop gain in dB on the vertical axis, open-loop phase in degrees on the horizontal axis, with M and N contours overlaid. Show how to plot G(jω) point by point, read closed-loop M and N, and find resonant peak Mr, resonant frequency ωr and bandwidth. Some syllabi write Nichol's chart.

figure.aria: Constant-M circles for M=2 and M=4 in the open-loop plane; the point for G(j2) lies inside the M=2 circle and just outside the M=4 circle.

chapters.example: For G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)), at ω=2 rad/s, G(j2)=−1.058−j0.289. Find closed-loop M and N by T=G/(1+G), and state where the point lies relative to the M=2 and M=4 circles. Answer: T=3.73∠−63.4°, so M=3.73 (11.4 dB), N=−63.4°; the point lies inside the M=2 circle and outside the M=4 circle.
chapters.trap: M circles live in the open-loop G-plane, not the closed-loop plane. The critical point is −1. A point on the M=1 circle has closed-loop magnitude 1, not open-loop magnitude 1. Nichols chart axes are open-loop gain in dB and open-loop phase in degrees; do not plot closed-loop phase on the horizontal axis.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 Bode plot, 4.5 Nyquist plot, 4.6 margins; complex arithmetic.
chapters.leave: Detailed compensator design to Unit 5; exact time response to Unit 2.
